fixes.explanation: That's the one. Elihu asks Job, "Do you think this is just? You say, ‘I am more righteous than God.’" (Job 35:2) Those are Elihu's words about Job, and he puts them right on the table. I think that's a pretty heavy thing to say to a man who's hurting.

That one sounds like something a tough guy would say, but it isn't what Elihu quotes. He says Job claims, "I am more righteous than God." (Job 35:2) Strength never comes up in that verse at all. I'd have loved to see a stamper claim he's stronger than his troubles. Mine came with dust bunnies from the junk drawer I got stuck in for years.

Job's friends do come up in this passage, since Elihu says his reply is for them too (Job 35:4). But the question Elihu quotes in verse 3 is about profit and benefit. Nobody's being called harsh there. It's a payoff question, like asking what you get out of showing up early to work every day.

I get why you'd pick it, since Job is hurting (Job 2:7) and waiting is the whole mood of this book. But Elihu quotes something else: "What does it profit me, and what benefit do I gain apart from sin?" (Job 35:3) That's about what doing right gets you. A question about when it ends would sound a lot different.

Right on. Elihu says, "I will reply to you and to your friends as well." (Job 35:4) So Job isn't the only one getting an answer. His friends are in it too. That's a full kitchen, and everybody's getting a plate.

Job did have servants earlier in the story (Job 1:15), but Elihu isn't talking to them here. He says, "I will reply to you and to your friends as well." (Job 35:4) The friends are the ones he names. Servants don't show up in this verse at all.

Yes. Elihu says, "There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) Notice who the pride belongs to: evil men, not the ones crying out. That's Elihu's claim about why the cries go unanswered, and I'd keep it right there in his words.

That's right. Elihu says, "Surely God does not listen to empty pleas, and the Almighty does not take note of it." (Job 35:13) He's saying that pleas with nothing behind them don't get God's ear. Listen is the first blank, and it pairs with empty in the second.

Yes, empty is the word. Elihu says, "Surely God does not listen to empty pleas…" (Job 35:13) Empty is his label for the kind of pleas he says God doesn't listen to. Put it with listen and you've got his whole point.

Actually, it's the other way around. Elihu says, "How much less, then, when you say that you do not see Him, that your case is before Him and you must wait for Him…" (Job 35:14) He's just said God doesn't listen to empty pleas. Now he says Job's words about not seeing God deserve even less of God's attention, not more.

Yes, that's the right call. Elihu says, "How much less, then, when you say that you do not see Him, that your case is before Him and you must wait for Him…" (Job 35:14) He's building on the empty pleas of verse 13. His point is that Job's words about not seeing God get even less of God's attention, not more.

Yep. Elihu finishes with, "So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge." (Job 35:16) That's the last thing he says in this passage. I think it's a hard thing to hear when you're already hurting (Job 2:7).
